summary.text: An ice age is a long stretch when a colder surface and atmosphere keep Earth's alpine glaciers and polar ice caps in place or growing.
Within an ice age, colder spells called glacials alternate with relatively warmer spells called interglacials.
For most of its history Earth has had little or no permanent ice, yet it is in an ice age right now, the Late Cenozoic Ice Age that began 34 million years ago.

facts.label: Current ice age
facts.value: Late Cenozoic Ice Age, began 34 million years ago

facts.label: Early clue
facts.value: Stray boulders that Alpine locals blamed on past glaciers

items.prompt: When Pierre Martel visited an Alpine valley in 1742, locals had an explanation for the huge stray boulders there. What was it?

options.label: A great flood had swept them down
The glaciers had once reached much farther
Volcanoes had hurled them there
Ancient builders had dragged them in

items.explain: The valley's inhabitants credited the glaciers, saying they had once extended much farther than they did then.

items.prompt: In 1818 an ice-dammed lake in a Swiss valley finally burst. The flood left only small boulders and no scratches in the rock. What did Ignatz Venetz conclude?

options.label: Floods had made the valley's giant boulders after all
The boulders must have come from a landslide
The scratches were made by much older floods
Only ice could explain the giant boulders and scratches

items.explain: Since a real flood produced nothing like the giant erratics and rock scratches, Venetz decided only ice could have caused them.

items.prompt: In 1824 Jens Esmark argued that a sequence of worldwide ice ages had a single kind of cause. What did he point to?

options.label: Changes in Earth's orbit
Giant volcanic eruptions
Huge floods from melting lakes
Shifts in the Moon's tides

items.explain: Esmark proposed climate change as the cause and tried to show it came from changes in Earth's orbit.

items.prompt: Today we live in the warm Holocene, and permanent ice still sits at the poles. How do geologists describe this moment?

options.label: The ice age ended 11,700 years ago
Earth is in a greenhouse period with no ice age
A warm spell inside an ice age still under way
An ice age is due to begin within centuries

items.explain: Earth is still in the Late Cenozoic Ice Age; the Holocene is the current warm stretch within it.

items.prompt: Ice sheets shrink and the climate warms for thousands of years, but the ice age as a whole is not over. What is that stretch called?

options.label: A glacial
A greenhouse period
A glacial maximum
An interglacial

items.explain: The relatively warmer sub-periods of an ice age are interglacials; the colder ones are glacials.

items.prompt: Picture Earth across its whole history. What has the planet's usual state been?

options.label: Little or no permanent ice anywhere
Ice caps at both poles, as today
Ice covering most continents
Constant swings between glacials every few centuries

items.explain: For most of Earth's history it has been in a greenhouse period with little or no permanent ice.

pack.title: Boulders in the Wrong Place
pack.question: How did people work out that glaciers once covered far more land than they do now?

beats.title: Boulders in the Wrong Place
beats.hook: Giant stray boulders dotted Alpine valleys, and the people living there had an explanation long before many scientists accepted it.

beats.prompt: In 1818 an ice dam above a Swiss valley holds back a lake. The geologist Charpentier thinks floods moved the valley's giant boulders and scratched its rocks. The dam breaks and the lake floods out. What does the flood leave behind?
beats.explain: The flood left only minor erratics and no striations, so Venetz concluded only ice could have produced the big ones.

choices.label: Giant boulders and deep scratches, just like the old ones
choices.feedback: Tempting if floods really did the work, but that is not what the flood left.

choices.label: Only minor boulders and no scratches in the rock
A thick sheet of new ice across the valley
choices.feedback: Floods carry water and debris; they do not lay down ice sheets.

beats.prompt: Put these steps toward the idea of ice ages in date order.

items.label: Pierre Martel visits the Chamonix valley
James Hutton explains Alpine boulders by glaciers
Perraudin blames glaciers for boulders in Val de Bagnes
Jens Esmark proposes climate change as the cause

beats.explain: Martel visited in 1742, Hutton wrote in 1795, Perraudin spoke up in 1815 and Esmark published in 1824.

beats.prompt: Match each thinker to the idea they put forward.

right.label: Polar ice caps once reached the temperate zones
Scandinavia was glaciated, as a regional event
Drifting sea ice carried the boulders
Worldwide ice ages driven by orbit changes

beats.explain: Each was trying to explain the same evidence, but they disagreed on how far the ice reached and why.

beats.prompt: Sort each stretch of time by whether it was a cold spell or a warm spell.
beats.explain: Glacials and glaciations like the Last Glacial Maximum and Younger Dryas are the cold phases; interglacials and the Holocene are the warmer ones.

beats.idea: Stray boulders and scratched rock convinced investigators that ice, not floods, once spread far beyond today's glaciers.

paragraphs.heading: What an ice age is
paragraphs.text: An ice age is a stretch of time when Earth's surface and air are colder, so glaciers and polar ice caps last a long time or spread. People use the name both for very long cooling periods and for fairly short ones. Within one ice age, temperature and the amount of ice can swing back and forth. The colder spells are called glacials, and the relatively warmer ones are called interglacials.

paragraphs.heading: Icehouse and greenhouse
paragraphs.text: Over its history Earth switches between icehouse periods, when it has glaciers, and greenhouse periods, when it does not. For most of that history it has been in a greenhouse state with little or no permanent ice. Right now, though, it is in an icehouse called the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, which began 34 million years ago. The term ice age is also used for the Quaternary glaciation, which began 2.58 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: The most recent swings
paragraphs.text: The Last Interglacial ended 115,000 years ago. The Last Glacial Period came next, and its harshest stretch, the Last Glacial Maximum, peaked between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. The most recent glaciation was the Younger Dryas, from 12,800 to 11,700 years ago. Then the present warm interval, the Holocene, began 11,700 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from stray boulders
paragraphs.text: In 1742 the Geneva engineer and geographer Pierre Martel visited the Chamonix valley in the Alps. In his account two years later, he wrote that locals blamed the scattered erratic boulders on glaciers that had once reached much farther. In 1815 a carpenter and chamois hunter, Jean-Pierre Perraudin, gave the same explanation for boulders in the Val de Bagnes in Switzerland. Similar views turned up far away too: in the Chilean Andes in 1849–1850, local people told the naturalist Ernst von Bibra that old moraines were the work of glaciers.

paragraphs.heading: Scholars take up the idea
paragraphs.text: European scholars, meanwhile, wondered how the erratic material had been spread around, and from the mid-18th century some saw ice as the carrier. In 1742 the Swedish mining expert Daniel Tilas became the first to propose drifting sea ice as the reason for erratic boulders in Scandinavia and the Baltic. In 1795 James Hutton explained Alpine boulders by glacier action, and in 1818 Göran Wahlenberg described a glaciation of the Scandinavian peninsula, which he saw as a regional event. The geologist Jens Esmark went further and argued for a series of worldwide ice ages. In an 1824 paper he blamed changes in climate and tried to trace them to changes in Earth's orbit.

paragraphs.heading: A dam bursts
paragraphs.text: In 1815 Perraudin tried to win over the geologist Jean de Charpentier, pointing to deep scratches in the rock and giant boulders. Charpentier believed vast floods had left these marks and dismissed the idea as absurd. In 1818 the engineer Ignatz Venetz joined them to inspect a lake held back by an ice dam above the valley. When the dam broke it left only minor boulders and no scratches, so Venetz decided that only ice could explain the bigger signs. Charpentier, converted as well, published Venetz's paper with his own in 1834.

paragraphs.heading: Times of frozen water
paragraphs.text: Around the same time the German botanist Karl Friedrich Schimper was studying mosses on erratic boulders in the Bavarian uplands, and he began to ask where the stones had come from. After trips into the Bavarian Alps in the summer of 1835, he concluded that ice had carried them. He then proposed that the whole world had passed through cold periods of frozen water, which he called Verödungszeiten, or times of obliteration.
